questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvalue of a Matrix Given a Complex Eigenvector
questions.problem:
Determine if $v=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
questions.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors are non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3+4\text{i} \\ -4-3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{\text{i}}^{2}+4\text{i} \\ -4-3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\text{i}(4+3\text{i}) \\ (-1)(4+3\text{i})\end{aligned}] \\  & =(4+3\text{i})[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =(4+3\text{i})v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=(4+3\text{i})v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =4+3\text{i}.$

questions.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2+3\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =2+3\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 2+3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-3\text{i} & 5 \\ -2 & -1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(1-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+(-1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(2+3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}(1+3\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}(1+3\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=-\frac{1+3\text{i}}{2}=-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3}{2}\text{i}.$

questions.problem:
Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].$
Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1-3\text{i} & 5 \\ -2 & 1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-1-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-3\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{1}{5}(1+3\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ \frac{1}{5}(1+3\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1+3\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the  complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=-3\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}=\frac{(5)(5)}{(1+3\text{i})(1-3\text{i})}=\frac{5}{2}.
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-2+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=-4\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the  complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=4\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2-\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}=\frac{(-2+\text{i})(-2-\text{i})}{(1)(1)}=5.
$$

questions.problem:
Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-6-\lambda  & -4 \\ 5 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-6-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-(-4)(5) & =0 \\ -12+6\lambda -2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{-4\pm \sqrt{{4}^{2}-4(1)(8)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-4\pm 4\text{i}}{2} \\  & =-2\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =-2\pm 2\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2+2\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4-2\text{i} & -4 \\ 5 & 4-2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-4-2\text{i}){x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{1}+(4-2\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-2+2\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-1-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-1-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=2,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2-\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2-2\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}} & =\frac{(2)(2)}{(-2-\text{i})(-2+\text{i})}=\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Determine whether ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/59af73d1cda1a988c775ccf198b53653b96660b4ad8416add1b0c1816e89a5a5.png) is an eigenvector of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070616/assets/963bcaf94bc481fe8fbc99ca28fba037047d8821661eadcf0e5e9ce50ba39ef8.png)
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $\mathbf{v}$ such that $A\mathbf{v}=\lambda \mathbf{v}.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ 8 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-18+6\text{i} \\ 24\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18{\text{i}}^{2}+6\text{i} \\ 24\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =6\text{i}[\begin{aligned}1+3\text{i} \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =6\text{i}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A\mathbf{v} = 6\textrm{i} \mathbf{v},$ we conclude that $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda=6\textrm{i}.$
